RSS was introduced by Aleksandr Petrov and Craig Macdonald in “Effective and Efficient Training for Sequential Recommendation using Recency Sampling” (RecSys 2022). For positions k=0,…,n−1, it samples c=max(1,⌊τn⌋) target positions with replacement using p(k)=f(k)/Σf(j), originally f(k)=α^(n−k). Duplicates collapse into a target set; consequently, position inclusion probability is 1−(1−p(k))^c, distinct from per-draw probability. The endpoint follows the same distribution, without a reserved 0.1 mass. RSS removes sampled positions and retains the remaining sequence in order: this is generally not a strict prefix and can retain interactions occurring after a target. [Original paper, §4 and Algorithm 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.02643).

For the proposed policy, let N be the number of eligible nonterminal cutoffs and m=min(10,N). Assuming the recent window excludes the endpoint, its unconditional probabilities are q(endpoint)=0.1 and q(k)=0.45/N+0.45·1[k in recent window]/m. Thus older cutoffs have a uniform probability floor, recent cutoffs receive a constant bonus, and the endpoint has separately controlled mass. A cutoff example uses only the preceding history plus a reserved mask, predicting the withheld next item; this differs materially from RSS’s multiple-target deletion construction. These probabilities follow from the supplied policy, rather than a published standard BERT4Rec recipe.

RSS supports multiple-positive losses and evaluates BCE and LambdaRank; its probability normalization is not loss normalization. The supplied proposal does not specify whether loss averages over examples, masked targets, or first within each sequence, so that comparison remains unresolved. Assessment: recency-biased supervision is established prior art; the concrete mixture, endpoint treatment and prefix construction distinguish this implementation, but meaningful empirical novelty requires controlled ablations.
